content: The infection associated with a hordeolum can be either internal or external. In many instances, a hordeolum may resolve spontaneously without the need for medical intervention. However, the inflammation can potentially spread to other ocular glands or recur. Causes A stye is most commonly caused by the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus. It can be triggered by factors such as stress, poor nutrition, or insufficient sleep. Additionally, a stye may develop as a secondary complication of blepharitis. Differential Diagnosis It is essential to differentiate a stye from other conditions, including: Xanthelasma Papilloma Cyst Pyogenic granuloma Amyloid deposition Risk Factors The development of hordeola is associated with certain risk factors, such as: Dry eyes Chronic blepharitis Epidemiology and Demographics Styes are particularly common in infants, although they can occur at any age. Diagnosis History and Symptoms The initial signs of a stye include tenderness and redness in the affected area. Common symptoms include: Swelling Excessive tearing (watering of the eye) Sensitivity to light Discomfort during blinking Physical Examination Eyes A localized, tender area with a pointing eruption may be observed in the affected region. A yellowish bump may also be noted. Lymph Nodes Adjacent lymph nodes may be palpable. Treatment Medical Therapy Most cases of hordeolum resolve without specific treatment. Supportive therapy typically involves the application of warm compresses. Antimicrobial ophthalmic ointments may also be used in certain cases. 1. External Hordeolum (Single Lesion) Preferred regimen: Supportive therapy is usually sufficient. This includes the application of warm compresses 4–6 times per day. Note: The use of antibiotic therapy for a single lesion is of questionable value and is often not indicated. 2. External Hordeolum (Multiple or Recurrent Lesions) Preferred regimen (1): Bacitracin ophthalmic ointment applied every 8–24 hours. Preferred regimen (2): Erythromycin topical ointment applied every 4–6 hours. 3. Internal Hordeolum Preferred regimen: Warm compresses applied 4–6 times per day in conjunction with systemic antistaphylococcal antibiotics. Note: If the lesion does not respond to this regimen, incision and drainage are indicated.
